title: Typing React patterns
subtitle: Props, generics, useState trap, refs, events

cards.front: What does React + TypeScript interview coverage focus on?
cards.meaning: Mostly props, hooks, and events. Interviewers probe union-constrained props (not loose string), generics on list-like components, the useState literal-widening trap, reducers typed with discriminated unions, the two useRef overloads (DOM vs mutable box), and typing forwardRef plus DOM events.

cards.front: What TypeScript topics does React typing assume?
cards.meaning: Generics, unions / discriminated unions, and narrowing. Those are the tools behind List<T>, variant unions, and reducer action switches.

cards.front: How should component props be typed?
cards.meaning: Props are a normal object type, usually an interface. Optional props use `?`. Runtime defaults live in the destructuring (`variant = 'primary'`), not in the type system as default values.
cards.example: function Button({ label, onPress, variant = 'primary', children }: ButtonProps)

cards.front: What is React.ReactNode, and when vs ReactElement?
cards.meaning: ReactNode is anything React can render: elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null, undefined, and booleans (mostly ignored when rendering). Prefer it for children unless you need a stricter shape. ReactElement means a single element only.

cards.front: When type children as string instead of ReactNode?
cards.meaning: Use string when children must be text-only. Use ReactNode for flexible children and ReactElement when you require a single element.

cards.front: Why type variant as 'primary' | 'secondary' instead of string?
cards.meaning: Union literals make typos and invalid variants compile errors. string only fails at runtime (wrong CSS class). Small detail, strong signal in reviews.

cards.front: Does variant?: in the props type set a runtime default?
cards.meaning: No. Optional `?` only allows omitting the prop. Defaults belong in destructuring (`variant = 'primary'`), not only in the type definition.
cards.notes: Putting default prop values only in the type is a common mistake.

cards.front: How does List<T> stay typed without any in renderItem?
cards.meaning: T is inferred from items: T[] and checked against renderItem and keyExtractor. One reusable component stays typed for User, Product, etc., without any in callbacks.

cards.front: Do callers usually write List<User> explicitly?
cards.meaning: Rarely. T is inferred from items (and checked against callbacks). Write an explicit type argument only when inference needs a nudge.

cards.front: What type does useState('idle') infer?
cards.meaning: string — the literal widens. That will not catch invalid statuses. For a closed set, pass an explicit type argument: useState<'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'>('idle').

cards.front: Why does useState widen string/number/boolean literals?
cards.meaning: If TS inferred status as the literal 'idle', then setStatus('loading') would be a type error — the only assignable value would be 'idle'. Inference widens those literals to string / number / boolean for useState’s initial value so the setter is usable.

cards.front: When should useState stay string vs a status union?
cards.meaning: For a closed set of states, pass an explicit type argument (or as const patterns / const object maps). For open text (useState('') for an input), plain string is correct.

cards.front: Can object or array useState initials also be too loose?
cards.meaning: Yes — they can be looser than you intend. Annotate when the shape is a fixed state machine, same idea as status unions.

cards.front: How do discriminated union actions type a reducer?
cards.meaning: A discriminant like type narrows in switch so action.by exists only on increment/decrement branches, not on reset. Same pattern as Redux-style reducers. useReducer(reducer, initialState) then types dispatch to accept only valid Actions.

cards.front: How can a missing reducer case become a type error?
cards.meaning: With strict / no implicit returns, missing a case can error if you do not return State on all paths — good pressure to handle every action.

cards.front: What does useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) mean?
cards.meaning: Null-initialized element ref: React fills .current with the DOM node (or null). Typical for reading the node in effects and handlers. .current may be null until mount and after unmount.

cards.front: What does useRef(0) mean vs a DOM ref?
cards.meaning: Mutable-box ref: you read/write .current yourself for timerId, previous props, etc. It persists across renders without re-render. Changing .current does not trigger a render — do not use it when you mean state that should update the UI.

cards.front: Do interviews care about RefObject vs MutableRefObject names?
cards.meaning: Exact RefObject vs MutableRefObject wording has shifted across @types/react / React 19. Interviews still want the two intents: null-initialized element ref vs mutable value ref.

cards.front: What is forwardRef for?
cards.meaning: It exposes an inner DOM node (or child handle) to parents so they can hold a ref to the inner input, not just the wrapper component.

cards.front: What is the type-parameter order of forwardRef?
cards.meaning: forwardRef<RefType, PropsType> — ref element type first, props second. Easy interview trap to swap them (Props first by mistake).

cards.front: Does React 19 still require forwardRef?
cards.meaning: React 19 can pass ref as a normal prop in some setups; many codebases still use forwardRef. Know the classic generic order either way.

cards.front: How do you type an input onChange handler?
cards.meaning: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> so e.target.value is a typed string. Prefer these over any or untyped e, so e.target / e.currentTarget match the element.

cards.front: How do you type form onSubmit?
cards.meaning: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> for <form onSubmit>.

cards.front: How do you type a button click handler?
cards.meaning: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement> (or the element actually used).

cards.front: How do you type a keyboard handler on an input?
cards.meaning: React.KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>.

cards.front: For delegated handlers, target or currentTarget?
cards.meaning: currentTarget is usually the safer typed element — it matches the element the handler is attached to.

cards.front: Must you annotate event handler parameters in JSX?
cards.meaning: No. You can inline without annotating if the JSX prop context infers the handler type.

cards.front: Why not type React handlers as DOM Event?
cards.meaning: Bare Event from the DOM lib lacks the React generic element, so e.target / e.currentTarget are not tied to the actual element. Use ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> and similar.

cards.front: What are ComponentProps<'button'> and ComponentPropsWithoutRef for?
cards.meaning: They extend native element props instead of re-declaring className, disabled, etc. — a supporting pattern for wrapping DOM elements.

cards.front:
What does PropsWithChildren

add?
cards.meaning: It is P & { children?: ReactNode } — a helper for adding optional children to a props type.

cards.front: Can a click handler be async in TypeScript?
cards.meaning: Return type void | Promise<void> is fine. Do not pretend events wait on the promise unless you handle errors.

cards.front: Are ComponentProps and PropsWithChildren the interview core?
cards.meaning: No. They show up in practice as supporting tools. In interviews stay focused on the curriculum list: props/children, generic lists, useState widening, useReducer action unions, the two useRef overloads, forwardRef generics, and event handler types.

cards.front: Why is any on list renderItem a mistake?
cards.meaning: It throws away the item type. Use a generic List<T> so renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode stays tied to items.

cards.front: How do union literals connect to React typing?
cards.meaning: Union literals type prop variants and useState status machines so invalid values fail at compile time.

cards.front: How do discriminated unions connect to useReducer?
cards.meaning: Discriminated unions plus narrowing type action objects so each switch branch sees only that action’s fields.

cards.front: How do generics connect to List and forwardRef?
cards.meaning: Generics plus inference type List<T> from items and type forwardRef<Ref, Props> with the ref element first.

cards.front: How does nullability show up with refs?
cards.meaning: ref.current is possibly null until mount (and after unmount), so you must account for null before using the DOM node.
